--- title: "Week 11 Self-Assessment" subtitle: "Introduction to Research Methods & DataLab" --- ::: {.cell} ::: ## Instructions Test your understanding of this week's material. Answer each question to check your learning. --- ## Conceptual Questions ### Question 1: Why Research Methods? Why is "common sense" unreliable for understanding human behaviour?
Common sense is unreliable because of: - **Hindsight bias** — events seem obvious after they occur - **Confirmation bias** — we notice supporting evidence and ignore contradicting evidence - **Anecdotal evidence** — individual cases can mislead - Common sense can justify contradictory conclusions (e.g., "opposites attract" vs "birds of a feather flock together")
### Question 2: Hallmarks of Science ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} opts_hallmarks <- c( "Popular, funded, published, and cited", answer = "Empirical, systematic, falsifiable, and transparent", "Theoretical, mathematical, complex, and reviewed", "Objective, simple, fast, and certain" ) ``` ::: What are the four hallmarks of scientific claims?
### Question 3: Variable Types A **continuous** variable can take any value within a range. A participant's **experimental condition** (A or B) is an example of a categorical variable. **Reaction time in milliseconds** is an example of a categorical variable. ### Question 4: Replication What does it mean for a finding to be "replicable"? --- ## Practical Questions ### Question 5: Measurement Error In the reaction time task (ruler drop), which of the following could cause measurement error? Inconsistent ruler height Participant knowing when the drop will happen Using a standardised ruler ### Question 6: Being a Participant and Tester Why did you act as both participant AND tester in DataLab? ### Question 7: Signal Detection In the staring task, what is a "hit"? What is a "false alarm"? --- ## Fill in the Blank Complete these statements: The four steps of the scientific method are: observe, , test, and conclude. A variable that can only take whole number values (like "number of words recalled") is called a variable. --- ## Summary Checklist Before moving on, check you understand: - [ ] Why psychology uses research methods rather than relying on common sense - [ ] The four hallmarks of scientific claims - [ ] The difference between continuous, categorical, and discrete variables - [ ] The steps of the scientific method - [ ] What "replicable" means and why it matters
